header:
Date: 2025-06-12 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood ML Eng); Anna Lee (LuminaSearch CTO), Ravi Patel (LuminaSearch ML Eng), Mei Chen (LuminaSearch Platform)
summary: Technical deep dive on embeddings and reranking performance and cost. Reviewed vector dimensionality trade-offs, batching and latency SLOs, KV/prefix cache behavior for reranking, quantization options (fp16/int8/4-bit), and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed to run pilot benchmarks on 3 datasets comparing Redwood Dedicated GPU and Private deployment. Follow-ups: benchmark spreadsheet, pilot scheduling, security docs.
topics: KV cache and prefix reuse for reranking
VPC/on-prem performance differences and KMS concerns
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Miles: Hey everyone thanks for joining, can everyone hear me?
00:04 Anna Lee: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Jordan.
00:07 Jordan Miles: Cool, quick agenda — we want to focus on embeddings/reranking perf & cost, specifically vector dims, batching, kv cache behavior for reranks, and quantization options. Priya will drive perf numbers.
00:18 Priya Nair: Hi team. I'll start with a high level — for embedding generation we see two parts: compute time per embed and downstream ANN search cost. On the compute side, model size and vector dim drive time. On GPU with fp16 a 768-dim model is roughly X ms per embed at batch 32, 512 is ~Y ms, 1024 increases nonlinearly. These are ballpark until we run your datasets.
00:42 Ravi Patel: Quick Q — our current pipeline uses 768-dim embeddings from an open model and Faiss HNSW for ANN, we're seeing 60ms per embed on CPU, which is too slow for our interactive UI.
00:55 Priya Nair: That rings true. On CPU you end up in the 30-150ms range depending on CPU type. On GPU fp16 you can be sub-10ms per embed at larger batches, but for interactive single-query latency that doesn't help unless you do micro-batching or async pre-embedding.
01:10 Mei Chen: For reranking specifically we do a two-stage: first ANN to get topK (usually 100), then dense rerank using cross-encoder or dot-product scoring with context. How does KV cache play into that?
01:22 Carlos Ruiz: Good question. KV cache is most relevant for autoregressive generation; for embedding-only pipelines KV isn't used. But for rerankers that use a decoder/encoder cross-attention flow you can re-use cached key/value states across candidates if you're scoring the same query across many candidates with shared prefix — that saves a lot of work. For example, if you have a cross-encoder that encodes query+candidate together, you can encode the query once, cache its KV, and then stream in each candidate. That reduces per-candidate cost by ~30-50% depending on sequence lengths.
01:52 Anna Lee: So for our setup with query length ~30 tokens and candidates ~200 tokens that's meaningful. We have 1k candidates per query pre-filter, then ANN reduces to 100.
02:05 Priya Nair: Right. Two follow-ups: 1) you want to tune ANN recall/efficiency to keep the topK small (50-100) and 2) leverage prefix/KV cache inside the reranking model where possible. Redwood runtime supports persistent KV across a request batch when candidates are scored in the same request, and there's also a batching layer that can group candidates across concurrent queries to improve throughput while preserving p95 latency via smart routing.
02:36 Ravi Patel: Smart routing? Can you explain a bit.
02:38 Priya Nair: Sure — routing considers latency SLO and model cost. For interactive SLOs you can route to lower-latency dedicated GPUs and use smaller models for first-pass ranking; overflow to higher-cost models only for long-tail quality cases. Also, if private deployment capacity is constrained we can fall back to hosted variants if allowed by policy.
03:03 Anna Lee: Our SLO is p95 < 150ms for the combined embed+ANN+rerank path. Is that realistic on GPU?
03:11 Carlos Ruiz: It's tight but plausible. Breakdown examples: embed generation 8-15ms on GPU (fp16) for 768-dim at small batch, ANN search 5-30ms (depends on index & hardware), rerank per-candidate scoring 3-10ms if you use a light cross-encoder or dot-product. For 100 candidates naive serial rerank is too slow; you need to batch scoring and/or use cached query KV and run candidate scoring in parallel. With batching and a dedicated GPU we can hit 120-140ms p95 in many cases.
03:44 Ravi Patel: What about vector dimension tradeoffs? We're currently on 768 because of recall, but cost-wise 1024 is more expensive.
03:51 Priya Nair: Dimensionality affects memory, ANN index size, and compute per dot product. ANN search cost grows with dim linearly and indexing cost too. We usually recommend experimenting with 512/768: 512 often good with tuned training and retrieval augmentation; 768 is a safe default; 1024 helps for high semantic fidelity but adds ~25-40% cost in both embed time and ANN CPU/GPU memory. For many customers 512->768 is best for cost/perf sweet spot.
04:22 Mei Chen: If we quantize embeddings — say 8-bit or product quantization for ANN — how does that affect accuracy?
04:29 Priya Nair: For storage and ANN, PQ and int8 encoding are common; PQ can preserve recall well if trained on representative vectors. For reranking step you want to use full float vectors for the cross-encoder; but for initial ANN you can use quantized indexes with minimal recall loss. Redwood supports hybrid approaches: quantized ANN indexes + on-the-fly re-compute for topK full-precision rerank.
04:53 Anna Lee: Costs — what's the rough unit economics impact of dims and batch size?
04:57 Carlos Ruiz: Rough example: embed generation cost per 1M queries varies by dim and batching. On GPU with fp16, batch 32 amortization gives lower per-embed cost; but interactive single queries can't always wait to fill a batch. For single-query latency, micro-batching or async pre-embedding of likely queries helps. Quantization (int8) for model weights can reduce GPU memory and increase throughput, lowering cost maybe 20-40% depending on model; but 4-bit quant can have quality regressions unless post-training calibration is used.
05:32 Ravi Patel: We also run on-prem for some PII workloads. How different are numbers on private VMs vs Redwood Dedicated?
05:38 Priya Nair: On-prem depends on GPU model, NVLink, PCIe gen, and driver stack. Redwood Dedicated uses tuned kernels and newer GPUs; Private can be identical if you deploy the same hardware and allow us to use our kernel optimizations. The main friction is networking and KMS for keys. If your nodes are older, expect 10-40% slower perf. We usually run a short benchmark to normalize numbers.
06:05 Anna Lee: What about memory for ANN at scale? We have 100M vectors.
06:10 Carlos Ruiz: For 100M x 768 float32 that's ~307GB raw; with PQ or IVF + PQ you can reduce this by 10-20x. Index type matters: HNSW memory overhead is high but has great recall and low latency; IVF-PQ is lower memory but might need more CPU for search. Many at 100M use hybrid: quantized storage + on-disk/SSD assisted retrieval and a small hot in-memory subset.
06:37 Ravi Patel: On the Redwood stack, can we run FAISS on our private infra or does Redwood manage the index?
06:44 Priya Nair: Both options exist: you can manage your index and call Redwood for embedding + rerank, or host the index in Redwood-managed infra. For private deployments we can install faiss/milvus on-prem as part of the package and coordinate. There are tradeoffs for ops overhead vs integrated telemetry.
06:59 Anna Lee: Let's talk numbers — can we see sample benchmarks?
07:02 Priya Nair: Sure. I'll read some recent Redwood microbenchmarks (these are representative, not your data):
07:08 Priya Nair: Embedding generation (768-dim) on A10G GPU, fp16: single synchronous request ~9ms, batch 32 ~2.8ms per embed amortized. fp32 is ~2x slower. int8 weight quantization can reduce memory and raise throughput but single-request latency may not improve significantly unless kernels are optimized.
07:33 Carlos Ruiz: Rerank cross-encoder (query 30 + candidate 200 tokens) on a p4d-like instance: scoring 1 candidate ~6ms fp16; scoring 100 candidates naive serial ~600ms but with batching (score 100 in 4 batches) ~25-40ms per batch plus overhead — total ~120-160ms depending on concurrency.
07:58 Ravi Patel: Those numbers align with our anecdotal tests.
08:01 Mei Chen: What about batching for rerank? We often try to score candidates in batches of 16/32. Any guidance?
08:06 Priya Nair: Batch size sweet spot depends on sequence length and GPU memory. For your candidate length (~200 tokens) we often see batch 16 or 32 hits memory sweet spot on A10/A100. Batch 64 might OOM unless you use fp16+gradient offloads. Redwood runtime dynamically selects kernel and batch sizing and can do continuous batching: it will hold a request for a few ms to group with others. That helps throughput but can add a few ms tail latency. You can configure SLO to trade small latency for better cost.
08:39 Anna Lee: So how do we configure SLOs in practice? We want p95 <150ms but prefer p99 <300ms.
08:46 Jordan Miles: We'll set up routes: critical UI calls route to dedicated low-latency pool with small batch windows (<=5ms) and larger capacity; background/async flows go to cheaper pools with longer batching windows. Redwood console exposes per-route p95/p99 and cost breakdown so you can iterate.
09:02 Ravi Patel: Any caution about kernel/quantization incompatibilities on on-prem GPUs?
09:07 Priya Nair: Yes — older GPUs may not support certain int8 kernels. Also driver versions and CUDA mismatches can degrade perf. For on-prem private deployments we do a preflight to validate libs, and for totally offline we provide a validated bundle.
09:24 Anna Lee: For ANN recall tuning — what topK values do you recommend for our 1k candidate pre-filter?
09:29 Carlos Ruiz: We typically aim to reduce to 50-150 for rerank. If your ANN recall at k=100 is >0.98 for target labels, that's good. If not, either increase dims or improve ANN accuracy (index params, PQ codebooks) or use hybrid re-ranking with lexical filters.
09:48 Ravi Patel: About cost math — can you give rough per-100k query cost comparisons hosted vs dedicated vs private?
09:54 Carlos Ruiz: It's approximate but: hosted shared (pay-as-you-go) higher per-token cost due to multi-tenant and overhead; dedicated reserved capacity can reduce unit cost by 30-60% depending on commit; private is variable — hardware CAPEX amortized may be cheapest at scale but ops/engineering/repairs add hidden costs. We'll put concrete numbers in the benchmark sheet.
10:18 Priya Nair: Also consider caching strategies to reduce calls: prefix KV caching for rerank, result caching for frequent queries, and embedding caching for repeating queries. Cache hit rates are often the biggest lever for cost.
10:31 Anna Lee: Our workload has a heavy tail of repeated queries from the same customers — caching could help a lot.
10:35 Jordan Miles: Action item — we'll include a caching assessment section in the benchmark template.
10:40 Mei Chen: Security: if we do private deployment with KMS, does the embedding service ever see keys?
10:45 Priya Nair: Redwood can be configured to use customer KMS/HSM for key material; in private deployment the control plane can be customer-managed. For hosted, keys are managed by Redwood unless you enable BYOK integrations via HSM. We'll send the security doc.
10:59 Anna Lee: Great. For pilot scope, what would Redwood need?
11:02 Jordan Miles: Ideally: 3 datasets (small: 1k queries, med: 10k, large: 100k samples), target metrics (p95, p99, throughput, recall@k), and access to a sanitized sample of data for index tuning. We'll run on dedicated GPU and on-prem if you provide node access.
11:20 Ravi Patel: Sounds good. We'll prepare the datasets.
11:23 Priya Nair: Quick deeper note on quantization for models used to generate embeddings: weight quantization (e.g., int8) helps memory and throughput but can change embedding distribution — that matters for ANN. We recommend validating embeddings similarity after quantization. For many models int8 has small drift, but 4-bit can be risky without calibration.
11:49 Carlos Ruiz: Another optimization: use asymmetric int8 for dot products on CPU ANN to speed search and use tiny re-ranking on GPU for topK. That combination reduces cost significantly.
12:03 Mei Chen: For our compliance team we also need audit logs of inference calls and data retention policies. Can Redwood provide per-request logs and configurable retention?
12:10 Jordan Miles: Yes — Redwood Console gives per-route traces, token-level breakdowns, and configurable log retention. For private deployments logs can be shipped to your SIEM or kept in-cluster per policy.
12:24 Anna Lee: Ok, last technical question — what's the best experimentation plan to choose dim/batch/quantization?
12:31 Priya Nair: 3-step plan: 1) run functional quality evals (recall@k, nDCG) at dims 512/768/1024 on a held-out set; 2) run perf microbenchmarks for embedding latency at single-request and batched modes on representative hardware; 3) run full pipeline pilot (ANN + rerank) for p95/p99 and cost using real traffic or recorded traces. We'll help with the test harness.
13:00 Ravi Patel: Good. Let's capture the dataset and schedule.
13:04 Jordan Miles: Recap of next steps: send benchmark template, security doc, schedule pilot. Any other questions?
13:10 Anna Lee: No, thanks — this was useful.
13:12 Jordan Miles: Thanks everybody. We'll follow up with the materials.
13:15 (meeting end)
